articles.title: Bids encouraged to keep famed Sir Stanley Spencer artwork in UK
articles.summary: Sir Stanley Spencer is synonymous with Cookham, where he was born, lived and set some of his work.
articles.body:
A painting by one of Britain's leading 20th Century artists must stay in the country in the hope that one of its galleries or institutions will buy it, the government said.

Sir Stanley Spencer, who was born and spent most of his life in Cookham, Berkshire, is probably best known for the series of artworks he created on the theme of resurrection.

The Resurrection of the Good and the Bad, finished in 1915, is the first piece exploring that topic and is an "immensely valuable" piece to use in the study of his work, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) said.

Bids for the painting, with a recommended price of £450,000, will be welcomed until mid-December.

The diptych – an artwork spread across two panels – shows the Good on the left and the Bad on the right.

The export ban for the painting was recommended by the Reviewing Committee on the Export of Works of Art and Objects of Cultural Interest (RCEWA) and accepted by arts minister Ruth Mackenzie.

Mark Hallett, a member of the RCEWA, said: "The Resurrection of the Good and the Bad is crucial to a better understanding of this central strand of Spencer's artistic practice and is deserving of a great deal more research.

"It is imperative that we try and keep it in the UK."

articles.title: 49 days before 9/11, a businessman took Twin Towers' lease; 25 years later, the rebuilding nears end
articles.summary: News News: Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks destroyed the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers, the redevelopment of the 16-acre site has entered its.
articles.body: Twenty-five years after the September 11 attacks destroyed the World Trade Center’s Twin Towers, the redevelopment of the 16-acre site has entered its final commercial phase, with construction now under way on 2 World Trade Center, the last office tower envisaged in the original master plan.The 55-storey tower at 200 Greenwich Street broke ground in July and is expected to open in 2031 as the new global headquarters of American Express. The nearly 2-million-square-foot building will accommodate up to 10,000 employees and will be the final commercial office building on the World Trade Center campus to be completed or under construction.For Larry Silverstein, whose company holds the development rights to several of the site’s towers, the construction marks the latest step in a rebuilding effort that began after he took the lease on the Twin Towers for $3.2 billion in July 2001, just weeks before the attacks.“New York has always been a city that refuses to walk away from a challenge,” Silverstein told The New York Post. “After 9/11, I made a promise to New Yorkers that we would rebuild the World Trade Center, commemorate those we lost [and] restore commerce to Lower Manhattan.”The road to the final office tower, however, has taken decades. Silverstein spent five years fighting more than 20 insurance companies over payouts following the attacks. The redevelopment was also complicated by the involvement of multiple government bodies, with 19 agencies at one point overseeing different aspects of the site.The first priority was to establish that Lower Manhattan could once again attract businesses and workers.Silverstein Properties rebuilt 7 World Trade Center, which became the first tower completed at the site after 9/11, followed by 4 World Trade Center, 3 World Trade Center and the redevelopment of the central World Trade Center complex, including One World Trade Center.The towers had to come first, in part, to demonstrate that companies were willing to return to the area before financing another major office development became viable. “Every one of these other buildings kind of had to be built first,” Dara McQuillan, chief marketing and communications officer for Silverstein Properties, told The Post.American Express gives final tower a path forwardThe breakthrough for 2 World Trade Center came when American Express agreed to become the building's anchor tenant and take ownership of the entire tower.The company, which has been headquartered across the street at 200 Vesey Street for nearly four decades, has deep roots in Lower Manhattan and lost 11 employees in the September 11 attacks.“We witnessed firsthand the tragedy of September 11 and mourned the loss of 11 cherished colleagues,” Denise Pickett, President of Enterprise Shared Services at American Express, said at the July groundbreaking. “When many questioned what the future would hold, American Express chose to stay. [With the tower] we reaffirm that choice, and our confidence in the future of this remarkable neighborhood, by building here once again.”The financing commitment came after much of the groundwork for 2 World Trade Center had already been completed. Excavation and foundation work was finished in 2013 as part of construction connected to the Oculus transit hub, meaning the latest groundbreaking did not involve starting the project from scratch.The building will feature more than an acre of outdoor terraces and gardens. Its next major construction milestone is expected to be the topping out of the tower around 2029.The wider World Trade Center campus is now about 97 per cent leased, according to Silverstein Properties.The redevelopment was guided by architect Daniel Libeskind’s 2003 master plan, which divided the site between the memorial and commercial space. The buildings were designed so their office-facing sides look towards the 9/11 Memorial, while retail, restaurants and other commercial activity are concentrated along the surrounding streets.With 2 World Trade Center now under construction, the original commercial vision for the site is close to completion.One major piece still remains unresolved: 5 World Trade Center, a proposed residential tower with roughly 1,200 apartments. The project remains stalled amid rising construction costs, with some costs reported to have increased by as much as 50 per cent, partly amid instability in the Middle East.“The Port Authority remains fully committed to delivering a world class tower at Site 5, including the goal of one third of the units being affordable,” the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said.For the World Trade Center, however, the construction of 2 World Trade Center marks a significant milestone: the last commercial office tower from the post-9/11 master plan is finally rising, 25 years after the attacks transformed the Lower Manhattan skyline.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? The mother of an 11-year-old girl from Cheshire has described feeling "overwhelmingly proud" after her daughter landed a role in the sequel to Practical Magic.

Harriet, from Macclesfield, won the part of young Antonia Owens, daughter of Sandra Bullock's character Sally Owens, after she travelled down to London for a round of auditions in June 2025.

Practical Magic 2 is the sequel to the 1998 fantasy romcom which stars Bullock and Nicole Kidman as witch sisters. The film also features actresses Joey King and Maisie Williams.

Emma said her daughter had "taken it all in her stride" and that the process had been "an incredible experience".

"It was very nerve-wracking," Harriet told the BBC.

She said she was "very excited" to have been given the part and that Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman were "lovely" to work with.

Speaking ahead of a private screening for friends and family at a cinema in Macclesfield, Emma said she felt "overwhelmingly proud" of her daughter.

"When I got a phone call from the casting agent they asked whether I was sitting down.

"That's when they told me Harriet had got the part - I couldn't believe it."

She said: "From recording the self-tape, to hearing that the casting directors wanted to see Harriet in person and going down to London, every step of the way has been an incredible experience.

"We got to go down to the Warner Brothers studios for her costume design and fitting, hair and makeup, and then going on set was amazing.

"Don't get me wrong, there's been nerves, but Harriet has taken it all in her stride."

articles.title: US declares end of largest recorded cyclosporiasis outbreak
articles.summary: The FDA says contaminated lettuce has been removed from the market after nearly 13,000 linked cases.
articles.body:
United States health authorities have officially declared the nation’s largest recorded outbreak of cyclosporiasis over, after contaminated iceberg lettuce sickened nearly 13,000 people across 21 states.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said on Friday it is confident that all recalled lettuce linked to the outbreak has been removed from the market.

The CDC has recorded 12,883 cases linked to the outbreak, including 570 hospitalisations and two deaths .

Symptoms of a cyclosporiasis infection usually appear about a week after a person eats contaminated food or drinks contaminated water, although they can develop as early as two days or as late as two weeks after exposure.

The most common symptom is frequent, watery diarrhoea, but the infection can also cause loss of appetite, weight loss, stomach cramps, bloating, gas, nausea and extreme tiredness.

The outbreak was traced to iceberg lettuce sourced from central Mexico by Taylor Farms de Mexico, which recalled all of its iceberg lettuce from the region on July 17. It initially drew attention to lettuce served at Taco Bell locations, but federal investigators later traced the implicated lettuce to Taylor Farms, which distributes its products to restaurants and retailers across the US.

At its peak, more than 1,000 infections were reported in a single day. By August, the CDC said reported infections had fallen to fewer than two per day on average.

The outbreak was part of an unprecedented rise in cyclosporiasis cases nationwide this year. Since May 1, nearly 20,000 laboratory-confirmed cases have been reported in the US, more than 16 times the number recorded during the same period last year. The previous record year was 2019, when about 4,700 illnesses were reported.

Michigan was the hardest-hit state in the lettuce outbreak and accounted for the two deaths.

The outbreak has renewed scrutiny of US food-safety controls, including the government’s ability to identify contaminated produce before it reaches consumers. FDA inspections of foreign food facilities have declined substantially in recent years.

The FDA is supposed to inspect more than 19,000 international food sites annually. The agency hit an all-time high of 1,700 in 2019, less than one-tenth of the target, according to the Government Accountability Office. The FDA did not inspect the Mexican farm implicated in the outbreak until about a month after the investigation began.

The Trump administration has also scaled back FoodNet, stopping the programme’s mandatory tracking of Cyclospora and five other pathogens. At the same time, the Food Safety Modernization Act rule designed to improve traceability of high-risk foods, including leafy greens, has been delayed until 2028.

The FDA said it has completed on-site inspections and sample collection at iceberg lettuce farms and a processing facility in Mexico, although laboratory analysis of those samples is still pending. The agency said it will continue working with state and federal officials in Mexico to investigate the outbreak.

articles.title: Surrogate who refused abortion over heart defect takes custody battle to US Supreme Court
articles.summary: She fled to Texas where abortions are illegal and now wants custody of the four-week-old baby.
articles.body:
A surrogate who refused an abortion request from the parents who hired her to have their baby has asked the US Supreme Court to intervene in the dispute over who should have custody of the baby.

McKenna West filed an emergency appeal asking the court to halt a previous ruling granting parental rights to California couple Omar Ahmed and Nausheen Gilkar.

Ahmed and Gilkar had asked West to abort the pregnancy after a scan at 20 weeks showed the foetus had a severe heart defect.

Instead, West - who has been supported by several Republican officials - travelled to Texas where nearly all abortions are illegal and gave birth to the child.

The BBC has contacted lawyers for Ahmed and Gilkar for comment.

West has since been pushing for custody over the baby, born last month with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a defect where the left side of the heart cannot pump enough blood to the body.

The condition often requires multiple surgeries, which are not a cure. Infants with the condition can have lifelong complications, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

After West travelled to the state, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton intervened in the case and won an emergency court order requiring that the boy receive medical care in the state. He had surgery soon after birth.

West said she denied the couple's requests to have the abortion after learning of treatment options and wanting to keep "this precious baby", according to the Supreme Court filing.

West has argued that the biological parents should not have custody because she worries they would not give the boy necessary medical care because they sought to abort the child after learning of the life-threatening condition.

In a previous court hearing, Gilkar said the baby - whom they named Rumi - was "our child" and "the love of our lives", according to the Associated Press. They said West travelled to Texas without telling them and blocked their access to medical information.

A California court previously granted parental rights to Ahmed and Gilkar, while a Texas court issued a restraining order blocking West from seeing the baby.

Last month, an attorney for the California couple said the child was in critical condition and seemed to be "suffering from potential complications".

West argued that without intervention from the Supreme Court, she would no longer have access to information about the child's medical condition. In the filing, lawyers for West suggested that the California couple could place the child in hospice care.

articles.title: British lawmakers vote down bill to allow assisted dying, in reversal of past backing
articles.summary: LONDON — U.K. lawmakers on Friday voted down legislation to allow terminally ill adults in England and Wales to choose to end their lives.
articles.body: LONDON — U.K. lawmakers on Friday voted down legislation to allow terminally ill adults in England and Wales to choose to end their lives. Following an impassioned four-hour debate in the elected House of Commons, the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill was rejected 286 to 270. The outcome was somewhat surprising given that an almost identical bill had passed last year with a margin of 23 votes. The vote brings an end to a two-year debate in Parliament about assisted dying, during which the House of Commons had backed assisted dying on two previous occasions. Their backing wasn’t enough for it to become law because it was effectively filibustered by unelected lawmakers in the House of Lords. Back in the House of Commons on Friday, the bill had proposed allowing adults in England and Wales who have fewer than six months to live to apply for an assisted death subject to the approval of two doctors and an expert panel. Many individual lawmakers relayed their own stories both in favor of and against the proposal. The government took a neutral stance, meaning lawmakers voted according to their consciences rather than along party lines. One lawmaker who was among those to oppose the bill, having previously backed it, spoke about how “nightmares” prompted her to switch sides. Janet Daby said she dreamed of “dying and death” because she had not been “entirely comfortable” with her former position. New British Prime Minister Andy Burnham didn’t vote because he said he didn’t want to “unduly influence the debate.” Opponents branded the bill unsafe and unworkable, citing concerns around potential coercion of vulnerable people and a lack of safeguards for those with disabilities. Lawmaker and cancer surgeon Dr. Zubir Ahmed also noted uncertainty around a doctor’s prognosis. “I have to be honest with you,” he said. “When I am asked to prognosticate as to whether someone has six months to live or not, I am as often wrong as I am right.” The leader of Catholics in England and Wales, Archbishop Richard Moth, called the bill “wrong in principle” and “deeply flawed. The Church of England’s Archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, also objected to the bill. Medical colleges, including the Royal College of Psychiatrists, had raised “serious concerns” about the bill, saying there were “too many unanswered questions about the safeguarding of people with mental illness.” Proponents of “ assisted dying “ — sometimes referred to as “assisted suicide” — had hoped it would mark the biggest change to social policy in the U.K. since abortion was partially legalized in 1967. The intention was to put an end to the practice of those near the end of their lives going to other countries, such as Switzerland, for an assisted death. Lauren Edwards, who reintroduced the bill to the House of Commons, said the rejection was “heartbreaking” but expressed hope that the issue will win parliamentary approval in the future. “Assisted dying will come in this country, as it is already doing all across the world, but not soon enough,” she said. “Parliament has dropped the ball today. It will be picked up again as it must be, because the law as it stands is simply too cruel and too unjust to be allowed to stand.” Other countries where assisted dying is legal include Australia, Belgium and Spain, with regulations on qualifying criteria varying by jurisdiction.

articles.title: Top Ukrainian official gives inside look at the war with Russia
articles.summary: Head of Office for Volodymyr Zelensky talks technology, deaths, and hope for how the war with Russia could end.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) EXCLUSIVE — Four and a half years after Russia attacked Ukraine, the war between the two countries continues to rage. But this is not just a regional war, according to Lt. Gen. Kyrylo Budanov , head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.

Budanov says we could be at the beginning of World War III, if peace does not prevail soon.

“North Korean troops are in Europe. Russia is supporting Iran that fights the U.S. and civilized countries of the Gulf. There’s a whole range of hostilities happening in various countries of Africa where you see the same players support one or the other side,” the official told NewsNation.

Despite multiple conflicts around the world, his focus is on Ukraine and finding an end to the more than four-year-long war.

In an exclusive, far-reaching interview with NewsNation, Budanov — effectively the chief of staff to President Volodymyr Zelensky and the former head of Ukraine’s military intelligence agency — paints a clear-eyed picture of the war, the importance of the relationship with the U.S., Ukraine’s stability after a period of internal strife and what he personally relies on to navigate life during wartime.

The interview was conducted prior to the U.S. delegation traveling to Ukraine , but after CIA Director John Ratcliffe reportedly visited Moscow.

Of the official’s trip to the Russian capital, Budanov says he views it as a “positive thing because you need to always be talking.”

He added he was glad Ratcliffe spoke with the Russians about a trilateral summit, because it shows that the U.S. is ready for it. Ukraine, he continued, is also ready but he does not believe Russia is.

This past weekend’s trips, by special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, to Russia and Ukraine to jumpstart talks is a step forward, though nothing concrete has come of it yet.

A Ukrainian source familiar with the discussions in Kyiv, said they “were productive, some new ideas were discussed, and the goal is to end the war by the winter.”

FILE – Ukraine’s military intelligence chief Maj. Gen. Kyrylo Budanov speaks during press conference in Kyiv, Ukraine, Feb. 23, 2025. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka, File)

Budanov said he would “love this war to end in a just way so the aggressor would be punished.”

He also acknowledged that whenever a ceasefire is declared, the territorial lines will be “formed by the real state of affairs, the real status quo on the front line.”

So, it’s possible Ukraine could lose some territory given Russia currently occupies sections of the Donbas region. He expects the end to fighting to come with the help and mediation of the U.S., and specifically Trump.

In the meantime, the war is at a stalemate, the lieutenant general noted, adding, “Russia is not getting any strategic advances on the battlefield.”

He explained that Moscow may get “certain tactical gains, but we are getting certain tactical gains, too.”

“That is the reason why Russia switched to ordinary tactics of drone and missile terror against civilian populations and against civilian infrastructure,” Budanov continued.

Wednesday, a Russian drone struck near a mall killing at least two and wounding 14 others. Another strike hit a residential apartment building in Kyiv killing one person and injuring seven, including two children. There have been regular fatal attacks against civilians by Russia.

When asked if Ukraine would change tactics and target civilians as well, Budanov says, “we are not terrorists. And we’re only targeting legitimate military targets.”

Ukraine has focused their attacks on oil refineries, factories and warehouses, adding an economic strain to the attacks.

Zelensky said Ukrainian forces on Wednesday struck targets including a naval base and terminal for loading oil, as well as military port facilities and warships carrying missiles in Russia’s Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk and in the Krasnodar region.

Firefighters put out a fire after a Russian drone hit a gas station in Kyiv, Ukraine, Friday, Sept. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)

A United Nations report shows the agency verified at least 16,000 Ukrainian civilian deaths between the start of the war on Feb. 24, 2022 through July 2026.

That number likely doesn’t reflect all deaths, with unconfirmed deaths reported and incomplete information from some areas. Since the July report, the number has increased.

Available data shows far more Ukrainian citizens are dying than Russian citizens.

According to The New York Times, which cites the tracking group Conflict Intelligence Team , in the first seven months of this year, 327 civilians died in Russia from attacks. In Ukraine, the number was 1,695 civilians.

FILE – Ukrainian Air Force’s F-16 fighter jets fly over a Patriot Air and Missile Defense System in an undisclosed location in Ukraine, on Aug. 4, 2024. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky, File)

Budanov explained that one challenge for Ukraine is defending itself against Russia’s use of ballistic missiles, which are harder to intercept without a Patriot missile system .

Ukraine has asked the Trump administration for more missiles, and there has been talk of U.S. defense companies licensing the technology.

The official told NewsNation, “I’m not saying give that to us as a gift. I’m saying sell to us.”

“It is the civilian population who die because of those Russian ballistic missiles and Russian drones … We need those interceptor missiles to protect our women and children, to protect the future of this country,” he added.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky looks on during his meeting with President Trump on the sidelines of the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, on July 8, 2026.

Ukraine’s leaders are aware that Russia may be preparing a large mobilization, which likely includes drafting more Russians to fight. The Kyiv Post reports Russia is preparing to send up to 400,000 troops to the front in large part to take the Donbas, a region of Ukraine that Russia is contesting.

“I can say that nothing good comes out of it for Ukraine, but I can also say that for Russia, it will only end with a huge increase in [the] number of dead bodies,” Budanov said in the interview. ” It will be another challenge for our defense industry here in Ukraine.”

He continued, “Because we’ll have to significantly increase the production of drones that are used to kill the enemy and also projectiles and shells of various types. Because we need to be saving our soldiers.”

Should Ukraine need to mobilize further, the general says, “there is, of course, a degree of tiredness among the population, but still, thank God, the population understands that a collapse at the front line means a collapse of statehood.”

Working in Russia’s favor is their large population, something Budanov acknowledges. According to Worldometer , there are about 143 million people in Russia to Ukraine’s 40 million. With so many people, Moscow can afford to lose more and replace them quickly on the battlefield.

Ratcliffe has said the life expectancy of a Russian soldier at the front lines is just 30 minutes. More often than not, they’re killed by a drone.

The general noted that Ukraine’s technological adaptation has kept them in the fight and started to turn the tide of the war. He added that technologically well-equipped personnel can repel attacks of a larger enemy force.

Ukraine has arguably become the best in the world at drone warfare. Zelensky hopes the country will produce up to 10 million this year.

Budanov said the future will include more automation, more reliance on cyber systems, further integration of AI and more automated weapons systems.

“But still, the role of a human soldier at the battlefield, it will stay and it will remain,” he added.

While the U.S. has issued sanctions against Russia, a new bill that passed the Senate would be far more punitive in the hopes of pushing Russia to the negotiating table and ending the war.

Originally ushered by the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), the bill would, in part, allow the president to impose economic pressure via a tariff of up to 100 percent on all goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, as well as countries helping Russia evade oil sanctions.

“We have high hopes for this bill. And to my personal opinion, this very bill is a large advantage to the U.S. and the presidency in particular,” Budanov says.

He believes it would provide leverage to the institution of the presidency, and in this case, Trump could add or remove tariffs depending on whether Russia’s President Vladimir Putin listens to him.

It is exactly that power that has some Democratic House leaders concerned. Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, explained that he and other Democrats support Ukraine and want to punish Russia, but believe their bill is more effective because it would mandate the sanctions, Trump couldn’t waive them and it would address humanitarian aid as well as munitions support.

Perhaps most importantly to Meeks, he pointed to the institution of Congress while telling NewsNation they are the ones “that deal with tariffs.”

“That’s what the Constitution says…we should not be giving that authority away to any president, Democrat or Republican,” the New York lawmaker added.

Meeks said he’s open to a conversation with Zelensky and would even travel to Ukraine for it. With the midterm elections around the corner, it is unlikely the current bill will advance past the House floor, leaving the issue of harsher sanctions against Russia unresolved.

FILE – Ukraine’s former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov speaks to journalists during a joint press conference with Sweden’s Defense Minister Pal Jonson in Kyiv, Ukraine, Wednesday, July 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky, file)

In mid-July, Zelensky fired then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov in a move that was seen as favoring top military commander General Oleksandr Syrski , who was considered more “old-school” in terms of his leadership.

Fedorov had focused on tech-driven warfare and was credited with being part of the turnaround on the battlefield due to drone dominance. He was also popular with many Ukrainians for focusing on rooting out corruption. Thousands of Ukrainians protested his firing.

With the protests, Syrskyi was not chosen as defense minister, and no longer has his role as Commander in Chief of the Armed Forces (in Ukraine, that position reports to the defense minister).

Describing Fedorov, Budanov calls him, “a person without military experience. I’m not even speaking about the live combat experience, I’m speaking about just the experience in the military, a person without such experience cannot be in charge of the military ministry.”

Fedorov’s replacement is Yevhenii Khmara , who has combat experience. Mykhailo Drapatyi is the new commander of the armed forces. Budanov says time will tell whether they’ll be effective butNA calls on Ukrainians to give them the chance.

Regarding the corruption Fedorov was after, Budanov says, “All the politicians are campaigning and getting positions using slogans of fighting corruption.”

He explained it is the minister’s responsibility to eradicate corruption. The general also points out there are anti-corruption organizations to help.

Budanov’s name has come up in an investigation by NABU, one of the anti-corruption organizations. He did not seem concerned, however.

“I’ve always had very deep respect for our National Anti-Corruption Bureau and Special Anti-Corruption Prosecution,” he said in the interview. “That’s why I’m convinced that they will find out the smallest details who’s to blame and what are the mistakes or what are the felonies that they have committed.”

A Ukrainian flag waves during the flag-raising ceremony to mark the National Flag Day at the WWII memorial in Kyiv, Ukraine, Sunday, Aug. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky)

Despite the war, life goes on. When asked what music he listens to on good days and bad, he laughed and listed hard rock, heavy metal (including Metallica ) and some classical. His religion, family and specifically his wife help keep him grounded and bring him joy.

“She always supports me and when she’s nearby I’m not afraid of anything,” he told NewsNation.

That laughter, though, seems rare, which is not surprising since Ukraine is fighting for its survival. Throughout the interview, Budanov referenced the importance of “human capital,” including the soldiers and civilians.

“Capital is something you need to take care of, try not to lose at least and try to increase at most,” the general continued.

His message to Trump and Ukrainian soldiers? Believe in Ukraine.

This marks their first visit to Ukraine since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. On September 5, the envoys visited Moscow, where they met Russian President Vladimir Putin. According to media reports, the meeting lasted more than three hours. articles.title: Iran says will discuss Strait of Hormuz with Gulf states on Monday
articles.summary: Iran’s Foreign Ministry says the meeting in Oman is to ‘promote better understanding among the countries of the region’.
articles.body:
Iran is expected to meet with Gulf states in Oman on Monday to discuss the Strait of Hormuz, the country’s Foreign Ministry announced.

In a statement on Friday, the ministry said the meeting is intended to “promote better understanding among the countries of the region and help strengthen shared regional security”.

Iraq and coastal Gulf nations are expected to participate, the ministry said.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei also said: “Iran remains committed to ensuring the security of navigation in the strait”.

For several weeks, Iran and Oman, which both border the Strait of Hormuz, have been discussing how to manage the future of the strategic waterway.

Since the United States-Israeli strikes on Iran began at the end of February, the strait – through which one-fifth of world oil supplies flows – has been disrupted and blocked by Tehran.

The ongoing blockade has caused oil costs to rise, with prices surpassing $100 a barrel earlier this week.

Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Sinem Koseoglu explained that Iran is giving the Strait of Hormuz talks a “wider political spectrum” by inviting other regional countries.

“For some time we heard Iranian officials say that the regional issues should be solved by the regional actors, especially when it came to Hormuz,” she said.

“So we are hearing from the Foreign Ministry that foreign ministers from the GCC [Gulf Cooperation Council] countries and Iraq will be attending this meeting on Monday and the meeting will be held in Oman.”

Last month, Iran and Oman agreed on a shipping route, mine clearing and short-term management of the Strait of Hormuz.

“Basically it looks like they came to the second phase because we heard Iranian officials saying earlier this week they agreed on the main script on the temporary shipping lane and this would be announced soon,” Koseoglu added.

‘Critical and dangerous’ pressure on Iran

Meanwhile, speaking ahead of the BRICS summit of emerging economies in India on Friday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said the world was going through a period of “unprecedented complexity”.

“Iran has been subjected to heavy sanctions in recent years; this pressure has reached a critical and dangerous stage in recent months following the military aggression by the United States and Israel,” he said.

“When a country is subjected to political and military pressure on its trade, energy, infrastructure and financial system, the repercussions extend beyond its borders,” Pezeshkian added.

Since the US and Israel launched the war in February and Tehran retaliated by choking off the Strait of Hormuz, the global economy has struggled.

Amid the ongoing closure of the waterway, the US has continued its naval blockade on Iranian ports.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hailed the blockade on Friday, congratulating US President Donald Trump on “the economic pressure brought to bear against the world’s greatest source of instability”.

“The people of Israel stand with the people of the United States and with President Trump in confronting the forces of terror. In the year ahead, we will continue to make the world safer for all,” Netanyahu wrote on X.

Separately, in a speech marking the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 attacks in the US, Trump reiterated that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.

“We salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror, the Islamist Republic of Iran, will never, ever have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.

images.caption: Oil tankers and cargo vessels are seen anchored off the coast of Oman, which is set to host a meeting with Gulf states and Iran on the Strait of Hormuz [File: Elke Scholiers/Getty Images]

articles.title: Former football booster club treasurer is accused of stealing $400K
articles.summary: Julie Hanway Molina, 56, is accused of diverting the funds to pay for her home mortgage, credit card bills and other personal expenses.
articles.body: It’s a game night for Aliso Niguel High School in Southern California, but this Friday, the booster club’s website posted a stark message about a former club officer indicted on charges of stealing more than $400,000 raised for the team. Smack above photos of players in uniform and the rally slogan “Football First, Family Always and Community Forever,” the Wolverine Football Club posted: “We are aware of the recent developments regarding the former treasurer. We have been cooperating fully with law enforcement throughout this process and will continue to do so.” The former treasurer, Julie Hanway Molina, was arrested Thursday at her home in Aliso Viejo in Orange County, California. She was arraigned in federal court on charges of defrauding the Wolverine Football Club, Ciaran McEvoy, spokesman for the U.S Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California, told NBC News on Friday. Molina, 56, pleaded not guilty and was released on $10,000 bond, McEvoy said. The indictment only identifies the organization that was defrauded as a not-for-profit volunteer organization whose purpose was to “promote and enhance a high school football program through responsibly raising and managing funds, coordinating effective team-building activities, and supporting all student players’ growth and development.” “We’re going after all fraud, big or small,” Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a social media posting. Essayli told KTLA-5 in Los Angeles that Molina is a professional CPA, raising concerns among investigators about whether there are other victims. He warned that others who have done business with her “should check their books.” Essayli acknowledged to NBC Los Angeles that the case isn’t one that involves a large sum of money, “but this is a big deal to the local community. That was a lot of money that those students and parents worked hard to raise.” His office said in a statement that the FBI is investigating the case. NBC News reached out to Molina’s attorney, who was not immediately available. The indictment alleges that from sometime in 2023 to November 2025, funds were diverted from the organization’s bank account and used by Molina to pay the mortgage on her personal residence and pay credit card expenses. It alleges that Molina emailed false treasurer reports to board members to conceal the unauthorized payments totaling $411,761.54. The indictment alleges that interstate commerce laws, which would elevate the theft charge to a federal offense, were broken to divert the money and falsely report account balances. It details four counts of interstate wire transmission of funds. According to one of the counts, on June 23, 2023, $131,523.54 was wired from the organization’s Farmers and Merchants Bank account in Laguna Hills, California, through Federal Reserve facilities in New Jersey and Texas, to “Mr. Cooper’s” account in Santa Ana, California, to pay money owed on the mortgage for Molina’s personal residence. McEvoy said “Mr. Cooper” refers to the mortgage company. In the three other counts, the indictment alleges that on three separate dates — Aug. 21, Oct. 30 and Nov. 26 — Molina sent emails that traveled from California through a Washington server with false reports of the balances of the organization’s bank account. The charges carry up to 20 years per count in federal prison. If convicted, Molina could face forfeiture of property and other proceeds traceable to the stolen money. The arrest reverberated in the community, among parents and neighbors of Molina. “I’m shocked,” Angela Dimitrov told NBC Los Angeles. She said she learned of the fraud from her son when she arrived at the high school campus for back-to-school night. Tony Delmarmol said his daughter played soccer at the school, “so I know what it’s like. You have to spend a lot of money for that.” Molina’s trial date is Nov. 2, in the court of U.S. District Judge Mónica Ramírez Almadani. Aliso Viejo Mayor Max Duncan issued a statement Friday expressing disappointment, “particularly because these funds were intended to support our young athletes and their experience at Aliso Niguel High School.” Duncan said Aliso Viejo is a community of many young families and “youth sports are such an important part of who we are.” He expressed support for the volunteers “who are now dealing with the consequences of an alleged betrayal of that trust.” He said the community will continue to support the football program and support its community and volunteers.

articles.title: 25 years after 9/11, how much has changed?
articles.summary: Twenty-five years after 9/11, how much has actually changed? 9/11 is one of those rare moments that divides history into a “before” and an “after.” On Ian Ex...
articles.body:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, how much has actually changed? 9/11 is one of those rare moments that divides history into a "before" and an "after." On Ian Explains, Ian Bremmer looks back at the attacks that reshaped US foreign policy, launched the war on terror, and ushered in an era of military intervention, mass surveillance, and profound geopolitical change. From the rise of China and Russia as security threats to social media and artificial intelligence reordering our politics and flow of information, the world today looks very different from the one we knew that September morning.

But some things haven't changed nearly enough. America is once again fighting a war in the Middle East without a clear endgame or exit strategy. The surveillance state born out of 9/11 is still expanding, now including private companies that can track our location and recognize our faces. Looking back on how much the world has changed in the last quarter-century, what did we learn from the past 25 years… and are we ready for what comes next?

articles.title: How US leaders remembered the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks
articles.summary: Trump drew parallels to the US’s present-day war against Iran, while figures like Abdul El-Sayed called for inclusivity.
articles.body:
A quarter-century after the attacks on September 11, 2001, officials across the United States have taken part in tributes and memorials to honour the 2,977 victims and those who risked their lives as part of the rescue efforts.

The incident is considered the deadliest “terrorist” attack in US history.

Four planes were hijacked. Two crashed into the World Trade Center, causing its Twin Towers to collapse. A third struck the Pentagon outside Washington, DC. And the fourth plummeted into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers and crew rose against their attackers.

Through social media messages, public speeches and appearances at ceremonies, US leaders on Friday took different approaches to remembering the lives of the thousands who perished on the fateful day.

US President Donald Trump chose to stay in Washington, DC, to observe the 25th anniversary.

During the attacks, 184 people died near the capital when American Airlines Flight 77 struck the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US military.

Trump opted not to attend a Friday ceremony at the World Trade Center site in New York, where all his living presidential predecessors were in attendance.

His vice president, JD Vance, travelled to New York instead. The ceremony at the World Trade Center has a policy of not allowing political speeches.

In his remarks at the Pentagon, Trump described what happened as “true evil”. He also paid tribute to those who died in the attacks.

“We will honour their lives, we will cherish their beautiful memories, and we will protect this country and its freedoms for every future generation,” Trump said.

The president also praised US troops as he appeared to link the 9/11 attacks with his administration’s war against Iran.

“We will never, ever forget. That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice. There can only be victory,” Trump said.

“We salute the service members working right now to ensure the world’s number one sponsor of terror – the Islamic Republic of Iran – will never, ever have a nuclear weapon,” he later added.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth also spoke at the Pentagon, delivering his remarks shortly before Trump’s.

He warned the audience to practice “eternal vigilance” against what he called continued threats.

“There are still enemies who hate us. Every day, enemies plot to curb our power and kill our citizens, including from Islamic terrorists abroad and at home,” he said.

He proceeded to seemingly use the 9/11 attacks as justification for the US-Israeli war against Iran, which started on February 28.

“Over the past six months, we have laid waste to the world’s most prolific state sponsor of terrorism,” Hegseth said, referring to Iran. “Our warriors have fought an Islamic theocracy that has wished us death for nearly half a century, that cheered on 9/11.”

He went on to claim that the US military has destroyed Iran’s defences and that the US controls the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for international trade.

Iran has stopped commercial traffic through the strait since the start of the war.

“We’re still sending terrorists where they belong, to hell, and tankers to the bottom of the ocean where they belong,” Hegseth said. “And we’re ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. The economic pressure tightens every day. We control the strait. We will finish this fight.”

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani attended the New York memorial service, alongside the city’s former mayor, Rudy Giuliani, who led the city through the attacks.

Before the event started, Giuliani shook hands with the mayor, despite previously calling on Mamdani not to attend the event.

Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, had recently come under fire from some conservative politicians and victims’ family members who said his presence at the memorial would offend them.

A Change.org petition garnered more than 100,000 signatures from those who wished to express concern about Mamdani’s participation.

Like all politicians attending the service at the National September 11 Memorial, Mamdani was not permitted to speak.

Instead, the mayor released a video on social media remembering those who were killed and challenging the public to honour their memory by doing good works.

“Twenty-five years later, we have a sacred obligation to those who were stolen from us. To care for one another as they cared for strangers. To live lives worthy of the sacrifices they made. And to build a city worthy of their courage. A city where we run toward one another,” Mamdani said.

On Tuesday, Mamdani also released a trove of previously undisclosed documents suggesting city officials tried to downplay – or even mislead – first residents about the dangerous air quality following the attacks.

Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed took to the social media platform X to honour the lives lost during what he described as a “cruel act of terror”.

El-Sayed is locked in a tight midterm race in Michigan against his Republican opponent, former US Representative Mike Rogers.

Michigan’s open Senate seat is considered a must-win seat for Democrats, if they hope to take back control of the US Senate.

Rogers has sought to create controversy over El-Sayed’s past comments about the September 11 attacks. He has pointed to audio of El-Sayed reportedly saying, “9/11 scarred our country in profound ways, but what we did after 9/11 scarred millions of other people.”

During the Republican Party’s first-ever midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, on Thursday, Rogers blasted El-Sayed, who is Muslim, for being sympathetic to terrorists. He also sought to highlight El-Sayed’s links to left-wing internet commentator Hasan Piker.

“I never imagined that, 25 years after 9/11, I would be running against somebody who campaigns with Hasan Piker, who thinks America deserved it,” Rogers said. “Yep, but here we are.”

On Friday, however, El-Sayed used his social media post to push back against Rogers’s attacks.

“Nothing can justify the murder of innocent civilians. Nothing,” El-Sayed wrote.

He also called on Americans to help build a country that was “more inclusive, more empowering, more just” in tribute to the lives lost.

“They didn’t just attack America that day. They attacked the idea of America,” El-Sayed said of the 19 al-Qaeda hijackers who participated in the attacks.

“The notion of a nation brought together by ideals where it doesn’t matter how you pray or if you pray at all. A place where freedom and commitment to justice bind us, even if at times we struggle to fully realise it.”

articles.title: California woman chased, fatally shot by illegal immigrant DoorDash driver who stalked her for months: DHS
articles.summary: DHS says Shalini Thakur's fatal Sacramento shooting was preventable if Biden administration immigration policies hadn't released her alleged killer.
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said a California woman was fatally shot outside a Sacramento County Panera Bread Tuesday by an illegal immigrant who had stalked her for months and was subject to a restraining order. articles.title: Kamala Harris claims GOP 'cheating' ahead of midterms, says she's focused on stopping the 'madness'
articles.summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris accused Republicans of "cheating" by redrawing lines and suppressing votes, telling Megan Rapinoe she's focused on winning midterms.
articles.body: Former Vice President Kamala Harris accused Republicans of "cheating" during an interview Thursday and said she was working to "stop the madness" by helping Democrats win the midterm elections. "Midterms, midterms, midterms, full-time occupying my thoughts, my mind and my work," Harris said. "We have to win these midterms. These — these folks are cheating. They're redrawing lines. They're trying to make it more difficult for people to vote so they won't vote because they are afraid of the power of the people. "And, so, I'm spending full-time working on doing everything I can to help people restore some balance in our government, which is, through the midterms, winning back Congress, the House and the Senate so that we can stop the madness," Harris told former women's soccer star Megan Rapinoe on her podcast, "What Are You Like?" KAMALA HARRIS DIVES INTO MIDTERM FIGHT ONLY TO GET ROASTED FOR NEVER HAVING 'AN ORIGINAL THOUGHT IN HER LIFE’ Rapinoe asked Harris about what brought her back into political and public life. "I don't know how to live and not serve. I honestly don't. I just don't. It's something I've come to terms with. I don't know how to, I just don't know a life without figuring out how I can help move the needle," she said. Harris said she wanted to restore "some sense of sanity" and a functioning government. "If Kamala Harris is upset Republicans are going after the illegals and fraudsters trying to vote, it makes you wonder if she's taking crazy pills again. Voter ID and proof of citizenship are common sense, but Democrats can’t win elections without cheating the system," RNC election integrity Communications Director Ally Triolo told Fox News Digital in a statement. FOX NEWS POLL: SIGNIFICANT SUPPORT FOR BOTH VOTER ID LAWS AND MAIL-IN BALLOTS Rapinoe also asked the former vice president if she had made a decision about running in 2028. "I haven't decided," Harris said. "From my perspective, '28 doesn't matter if we don't win '26." Harris said during an interview last week with MS NOW's Peter Alexander that she even supported Democrats who don't want her on the campaign trail with them, because, she said, they need to do whatever it takes to win. "Listen, Peter, we need to win, OK? Bottom line, we need to win," Harris said. "I have run locally, I’ve run for statewide office and, obviously, nationally. And these candidates know what they need to do to win, and I would expect nothing less. "I look forward to being on the trail and helping folks where I can be helpful, but we have got to put a check on this lawless administration and deliver what Americans need and deserve. Lower costs, affordable healthcare, affordable childcare, you name it. So, I support them in doing whatever they need to do to win." KAMALA HARRIS BACKS MAJOR CHANGES TO THE SUPREME COURT, ELECTORAL COLLEGE AHEAD OF POSSIBLE 2028 CAMPAIGN Rapinoe also discussed her experience as a female athlete. "I’m thinking about my own experience being a female athlete, and I went through, in the prime of my career, just the most historic time in women’s sports," she said. "I mean, it was crazy in the best ways. We saw a huge amount of progress, which has led into a pretty significant regression in terms of just equal rights and people’s rights in general. I definitely think those two are tied. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "It was for the longest time, you know, don't talk about women's issues," she added. "Same kind of thing. And then it was like, 'OK, we're just going to do something else.' And I always just felt like they're like they're not going to let us just win."

articles.title: Should You Hand Wash Workout Clothes? Laundry Experts Weigh In
articles.summary: Hand washing your gym clothes can help them last longer and smell fresher — but is it necessary? Two cleaning experts share when it’s worth it.
articles.body: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends on our timelines, like whether honey is good for your skin. It can be hard enough to find the time to work out — do you really also have to find the time to hand wash your gym clothes afterward? That’s a question that divides fitness fanatics and laundry obsessives alike. Some swear hand washing is the only way to make your leggings and moisture-wicking tees last longer and smell good, while others say throwing them in a washing machine is totally fine. But there may be something to the former’s longevity argument. “Many workout clothes are made of delicate synthetic materials, which can lose their shape or start to degrade if washed in too warm water or thrown about too vigorously in a machine,” says Sara Aparacio, resident cleaning expert and spokesperson for Homeaglow, a cleaning service. But does that mean hand washing is really the only way to wash your workout gear? I talked to Aparacio and Ashley Torres, cleaning expert and team leader at Karen’s Green Maids, an LGBTQ-led green cleaning company to find out the truth. Should you hand wash your workout clothes? The good news: for most of your workout wardrobe, the machine is likely fine. “Honestly, for your daily leggings, bike shorts and tees, cold water on the delicate cycle will likely suffice,” says Torres. “The times I do choose to hand wash items is when they are the ones where the stretch is absolutely vital, sports bras with molded cups and any item with mesh. Hot water and a rougher cycle is the downfall of stretch,” Torres says. If you’re really unsure, you can always check the label on your clothes before you do anything else. “Generally, it’s best to follow the care instructions on the tag,” says Aparacio. My husband’s running clothes are pretty stinky after he logs miles, and this detergent has been great at eliminating that stench. Formulated specifically for sweat-soaked synthetic fabrics, it cuts through built-up bacteria that regular detergent tends to leave behind, so his gear actually smells clean again — not just masked in a cloying scent. This Dirty Labs Detergent is versatile enough for however you choose to clean your workout gear. Whether you’re soaking items in the sink or running them on your machine’s delicate cycle, this hyper-concentrated, biodegradable formula gently cleans without breaking down stretchy fabrics — making it a smart pick for any method. Experts say that if you’re machine washing sports bras, putting them in a laundry bag can help protect them. These bags are big enough for tank tops and other small items with delicate details that could get damaged from being thrown around a machine. This Amazon Basics drying rack offers plenty of slots to lay out sports bras, leggings and tees so they dry evenly without stretching in the dryer. When you’re done, it folds down compactly for easy storage, making it a practical pick for small homes or apartments without extra room to spare. How to wash your workout clothes Whichever method you land on, both experts had plenty of practical advice for actually getting the job done right. I spoke with Aparacio and Torres about their best tips for washing workout clothes whether you are hand washing or using a machine. If you are hand washing, follow this guidance: Turn clothing inside out: “Always turn the clothing inside out, since the main things you’re looking to clean with sportswear are your own body oils and sweat,” says Aparacio. “So turn the clothing inside out so that the areas that come into contact with your body the most are cleaned the most.”Make sure clothing is dry: “If I am hand washing, I always make sure my dirty workout clothes are dry before I wash them,” says Aparacio. “It sounds odd, but this helps prevent pockets of bacteria or mold from lingering during the wash and actually helps many sportswear fabrics absorb the detergent properly.”Pick the right detergent: Both experts suggest choosing a detergent that is either labeled as gentle or for delicates or says it is specifically for hand washing. Then, you really only need about a teaspoon of detergent for it to be effective, says Aparacio.Soak your clothes: Fill the basin of your sink (or tub) with cold water (hot water can degrade delicate clothes), add the detergent and let your items soak for up to 30 minutes — this helps the detergent penetrate so it can really tackle that bacteria and odor, says Aparacio.Rinse carefully: After your clothes have soaked, drain the water and rinse them out with more cold water. Go easy when it comes to wringing them out, as that twisting motion can degrade the fabric, says Aparacio. Instead, she suggests folding the items and then pressing down on them to remove as much water as possible.Hang them to dry: To dry your clothing, lay them flat on a drying rack or on top of a towel, says Torres. If you’re using a washing machine, these tips will help: Check the care instructions: Again, both Torres and Aparacio say that the best thing to do is to follow the care instructions on the tag of your item. This should give you an idea of what cycle to run on your washing machine. Mostly likely, workout items will suggest the delicate cycle.Wash workout clothes solo: If you’re washing odorous gym gear alongside your regular clothes, that smell could transfer. To be safe, it’s worth washing your workout clothes separately from the rest of your laundry, or at least in a load with other similarly smelly items, rather than mixing them in with things like sheets or everyday outfits.Prep your items: If you are machine washing, turning your items inside out is still a good idea. Not only does this expose the parts that most need cleaning to the detergent and water, it can protect things like trim and other delicate details. You should also zip any zippers on clothing so they don’t catch on other items. Finally, if you are washing a sports bra, consider putting it in a laundry bag for further protection, says Torres.Pick the right detergent: Similar to handwashing, experts suggest using a mild or gentle detergent on your workout clothes. There are also a number of detergents on the market specifically for workout clothing — in liquid and powder formulas — which are a good option if odor is something you struggle with. Skip the fabric softener: Both experts I spoke with say you should never use fabric softener on workout clothing. “The layer of ‘softness’ can trap odors and bacteria and even block the pores designed into the fabric to help with moisture wicking,” says Aparacio.Don’t let wet clothes sit: As soon as the wash cycle is finished, take your clothing out to dry it. Letting wet clothing sit for long periods of time can lead to bacteria growth and odor.Dry as instructed: Again, look at the label. Some items may direct you to tumble dry them on low, while others may suggest hang drying only. If it is the latter, laying them on a drying rack or towel will work. Want more from NBC Selected? articles.title: Declassified documents show UK aware of Israeli war crimes for 24 years
articles.summary: UK Foreign Office files, public since 2024, record warnings about Israeli violence and rights abuses since 2002.
articles.body:
British diplomats condemned Israeli conduct in the occupied West Bank as a pattern of human rights abuses in 2002 – 24 years before London took a tougher stance towards Israel this week.

These decades-old condemnations are contained in UK Foreign Office files written during the administration of former Prime Minister Tony Blair while Israel undertook a brutal 2002 offensive in the occupied West Bank.

The files, released in 2024 and reported in a recent investigation by the website Declassified UK, record British diplomats describing a pattern of abuses by a state their own government would go on to arm for the next two decades.

Today, Blair sits on the Board of Peace that presides over Gaza, where Israel’s disregard for Palestinian lives and the rules of war has been demonstrated on a genocidal scale, while the UK’s newly seated leadership refer to Israel’s actions as “a stain on the conscience of the world”.

But what did the British government already know about Israel’s actions more than 20 years ago?

That record begins in March 2002, when then-Israeli Prime Minister Ariel Sharon launched Operation Defensive Shield in retaliation for a wave of attacks by Palestinian armed groups, including Hamas.

Israeli forces tore through the occupied West Bank, killing 500 Palestinians in a single month, mostly civilians, and injuring another 1,500.

British officials were deeply aware of the scale of violations committed by Israeli forces.

A Foreign Office official wrote at the time that Israeli military operations in the West Bank involved a “pattern” of “human rights abuses”.

A senior British army officer was more blunt, calling the Israeli military a “second-rate, ill-disciplined, swaggering and bullying force”.

“They routinely use excessive force such as firing at the ‘legs’ of stone throwers or at ‘car tyres’ with the inevitable stream of ambulances ferrying youths to hospital with fatal bullet wounds to the head and body,” wrote the officer who was unnamed in the files.

Those concerns were put to the Israeli government directly.

Lord Michael Levy, Blair’s special envoy, warned then-Defence Minister Binyamin Ben-Eliezer that there was no military solution, and that the campaign would only produce more suicide bombers.

The Israeli violations described in the files have only multiplied, even becoming routine across occupied Palestinian territory.

Officials also wrote of Red Cross staff threatened at gunpoint, and their ambulances not allowed to reach the wounded. Today, intimidation and targeting of medics has become standard operating procedure for Israeli forces and settlers.

The World Health Organization has documented 3,254 Israeli attacks on healthcare across the occupied Palestinian territory over 20 years, killing or injuring more than 4,200 patients and medical staff. More than half of those attacks – and the deadliest of them – have come in the past three years.

Armed with the knowledge of Israel’s systematic human rights abuses, Blair’s government did act.

In 2002, it secretly halted arms exports to Israel for a time, after confirming British equipment was being used in occupied territory in breach of guarantees given.

But no UK government has gone as far as that brief embargo since.

As Israel’s violence escalated, the British response to it has diminished.

When, in 2008-2009, Israel killed about 1,400 Palestinians during 22 days of Operation Cast Lead in Gaza, more than eight in 10 of them civilians, then-Prime Minister Gordon Brown revoked licences for weapons on Israeli navy missile boats.

When Israel’s 2014 assault on Gaza killed 2,251 Palestinians, among them 551 children, David Cameron’s government identified 12 licences for suspension. It also said it would act if hostilities resumed; it did not.

When Israel’s current genocidal campaign in Gaza had already killed 40,000 by September 2024, Keir Starmer’s government only suspended 30 of 350 arms licences for Israel. Campaign groups later reported thousands of munitions reaching Israel anyway. That toll now stands at 73,658 Palestinians killed, including 21,500 children.

That is the record Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government hinted it may finally break with, as the UK and 11 other countries this month backed restrictions on trade with illegal Israeli ⁠settlements in the occupied West Bank.

articles.title: Several Latin American leaders are looking to the Bukele model to fight crime. This country has another idea
articles.summary: Uruguay is developing a new “democratic” strategy to fight crime, deviating from the draconian security measures popularized by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele.
articles.body: Uruguay is ranked as one of the safest countries in Latin America but rising public concern about crime have forced its policymakers to develop a new “democratic” strategy for the problem. Their aim is to bring down homicide rates while deliberately deviating from the draconian security measures popularized by El Salvador’s strongman President Nayib Bukele. While the iron-fisted crackdown on crime by the self-declared “world’s coolest dictator” has significantly reduced homicides in El Salvador, critics say it has come at the cost of mass incarceration and the erosion of democratic rights. Uruguay – a country that restored democracy in 1985 after more than a decade under a military dictatorship – has rejected such an approach, despite many of its neighbors adopting it. “More police, more prisons and harsher sentences. Historically, that was the formula for failure. And it only made the problems worse,” says criminologist Emiliano Rojido, a public security policy adviser to Uruguay’s Ministry of the Interior. Instead, Uruguay has designed a 10-year-long project called the National Security Plan, which aims to tackle the issue with a whole-of-government approach instead of viewing it as solely a policing matter. The project was proposed by the left-wing administration of President Yamandú Orsi and developed with support from multiple parties. Uruguay’s Interior Minister Carlos Negro, who led the plan’s implementation, said his country wants it to be “democratic, republican and participatory.” He insists that it won’t rely on “authoritarian formulas or measures” like the Bukele model, which he said cannot be implemented in a democratic nation. The Bukele model in Latin America Crime-related insecurity is a looming specter over much of Latin America. A 2023 study by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime found that the Americas have the highest regional homicide rate in the world as well as high rates of homicidal violence related to organized crime. This has led to public anxiety and demands for drastic solutions. “The entire region has been undergoing a decades-long deterioration in public security indicators,” explains Diego Sanjurjo, a leading member of the Latin American and Caribbean Group for Security and Democracy (Glacsed) and former coordinator of Comprehensive and Preventive Security Strategies under the previous Uruguayan government of center-right leader Luis Lacalle Pou. “Illegal markets and criminal groups have been growing for decades, and the very few countries that were considered safe have also begun to experience serious problems, such as Uruguay, Chile, Costa Rica and Ecuador,” Sanjurjo adds. The United States has partnered with several Latin American countries to fight organized crime and has carried out dozens of military strikes on alleged drug traffickers. Secretary of State Marco Rubio visited Colombia, Ecuador and Peru this week to discuss security efforts. Faced with the rise in crime, some countries in the region – including Colombia, Ecuador and Argentina – are attempting to replicate parts of the Bukele model with plans to build large prisons and increase policing. The hardline model is credited for transforming El Salvador from one of the most violent countries in the world to one of the safest, with just 1.3 homicides per 100,000 inhabitants, according to its government. But the country’s considerable drop in violence has come at a high cost to human rights, say critics. El Salvador’s democracy has waned amid a years-long state of emergency, mass arrests without due process, allegations of torture (which the government denies), control of the Supreme Court and a constitutional reform allowing indefinite presidential reelection, according to Varieties of Democracy. Moreover, experts and officials say the Bukele model is not easily applicable in other countries – due to fundamental differences in size, geography, criminal activity, institutional structure and other factors – nor does it guarantee success. Uruguay is roughly eight times bigger than El Salvador, its economy is stronger and its danger index is lower, according to conflict monitor ACLED. Uruguay’s alternative strategy Rojido rejected the strategy of providing security by sacrificing rights. “We understand public security as the exercise of rights: the right to life, the right to property, the right to freedom. If we have to restrict rights to achieve security, something is wrong,” he said. Diego Sanjurjo, a member of Uruguay’s Colorado Party, warned that repressive security policies tend to be addictive. “You put 1,000 more police officers on the streets, but crime does not go down. Yet no one thinks of reversing the measure. On the contrary, citizens want more police officers … No one ever says: If this didn’t work, I’ll reverse it,” he said. “Almost every country in Latin America is on that train: an increasingly expensive security system that does not produce results.” Uruguay’s plan seeks to address the problem through multiple approaches. First, it treats public security as a long-term state policy, which will last a decade and “transcend terms of office,” Rojido said. Second, it stops viewing the issue as merely a policing matter and starts involving more government agencies along with civil society and the private sector, including security firms and tech companies. And third, it aims to base public policy on facts and evidence instead of rhetoric and demagoguery, according to Rojido. Uruguay is also receiving support from various organizations. It has created a group of international institutions to provide technical assistance and financial support and document the plan’s implementation “in the hope that Uruguay’s experience could also be useful to other countries in the region,” Rojido explains. Uruguay is also a member of Glacsed, led by former Costa Rican and Peruvian presidents Carlos Alvarado and Francisco Sagasti, which specifically seeks to “broaden and strengthen the conversation about how to confront organized crime with firm responses that remain within the rule of law and do not entail a return to authoritarian regimes,” says Sanjurjo, one of its leading figures. When are results expected? So far, Uruguayan authorities have been unable to reduce homicides, the vast majority of which are linked to organized crime. In the Uruguayan capital and its surrounding areas, the homicide rate over the past five years has ranged between 16 and 18 per 100,000 inhabitants, while nationwide it stands at around 10 per 100,000. It is a crime that has statistically increased over the past half-century and is Uruguayans’ chief concern, according to polls. However, other crimes have been steadily declining, including theft, robbery, gender-based violence and crimes in prisons, among others. “Of course, we are well aware of the scale of the challenge we are dealing with,” says Rojido. Experts warn that results will not come quickly. That is why policymakers say they designed the Uruguay plan as a 10-year strategy that spans at least two government terms. To that end, Uruguay has favorable conditions for establishing security as a matter of state policy, “such as permanent dialogue among the different political forces and a robust civil society,” says Rojido. “Because, ultimately, the parties have alternated in government, and none has been able to find solutions on its own,” he adds. They already know the alternative: people losing faith in democracy, and “magical solutions, shortcuts, and demagogic, populist, authoritarian proposals emerging,” he said.

articles.title: In 1950, Long Beach opened Veterans Memorial Stadium; sold to its city college for $1 in 1987, it is now being replaced by a $250 million, 285,453-sq-ft sports complex
articles.summary: US News: Long Beach City College has broken ground on a $250 million stadium and sports complex, starting a major redevelopment that will replace its 76-year-o.
articles.body: Long Beach City College has broken ground on a $250 million stadium and sports complex, starting a major redevelopment that will replace its 76-year-old Veterans Memorial Stadium with a modern 285,453-square-foot sports precinct. The redevelopment was officially launched during a groundbreaking ceremony at the college's Liberal Arts Campus. The historic stadium will be demolished to make way for a new regional sports hub, which is expected to open in summer 2029. According to official announcements from Long Beach City College and reports by local news outlet Long Beach Patch, the new 18-acre complex will include a 10,000-seat outdoor stadium, a 2,500-seat indoor arena, specialised track and field facilities, and dedicated football and soccer fields. The project is being funded through Measure LB, an $850 million facilities bond approved by local voters in 2016 to upgrade campus infrastructure. Veterans Memorial Stadium first opened in 1950 under city ownership before it was transferred to Long Beach City College for just $1 in 1987. For about seven decades, the 11,600-seat concrete venue served as an important sports and community centre across Southern California.Multi-purpose sports centre to bring facilities togetherThe new 285,453-square-foot sports complex has been designed to bring athletic activities together in one location. Previously, many of the college's sports facilities were spread across different parts of the Liberal Arts Campus. Along with the main 10,000-seat outdoor stadium and 2,500-seat indoor arena, the project will include training facilities, sports medicine and rehabilitation areas, kinesiology classrooms, administrative offices, basketball and volleyball courts, concession stands and a Hall of Champions honouring former student-athletes. “Veterans Memorial Stadium has been part of our community's fabric for more than 75 years, and as a former Viking football player, I know how personal this place is to so many of us,” said Uduak-Joe Ntuk, President of the Long Beach Community College District Board of Trustees, in a press statement issued by the college. “It has served as a gathering place for students, families, athletes, veterans, and the broader community. With the support of local voters through Measure LB, we have an opportunity to preserve that spirit and write a new chapter for Long Beach City College and the community we serve.”Dr Mike Muñoz, Superintendent-President of Long Beach City College, said the new facilities would benefit both students' academic and athletic development. “This groundbreaking marks a major step forward in how we support our student-athletes at Long Beach City College,” Dr. Muñoz noted in the press release. “This new complex will give our students access to modern athletic and instructional spaces designed to support their success both in competition and in the classroom. What matters most is what our students will be able to accomplish here, and I look forward to seeing how this investment helps them reach their full potential.” Project managers also plan to seek Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) Gold certification for the complex. The project will include energy-efficient power systems, recycled materials and sustainable water management.Demolition marks end of local sports eraThe stadium's history dates back to 1945, when 17 local soldiers serving in the South Pacific wrote to city officials asking for a stadium dedicated to local residents killed during World War II. The venue opened five years later in 1950 and soon became more than just a sports facility. During its seven decades of operation, Veterans Memorial Stadium served as the home of the Long Beach City College Vikings and Long Beach Polytechnic High School football teams. It also hosted regional track meets, high school graduation ceremonies, motorcycle races, roller derby, rugby matches, swap meets and commercial film shoots. The redevelopment began with site clearance and structural demolition. Architecture firm Gensler is designing the new complex, while Swinerton is the general contractor responsible for the first phase of demolition. Cordoba Corporation is managing the overall project for the college district. During construction, local high schools and college sports teams that regularly used the stadium will move their competitions and graduation ceremonies to other regional facilities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
