articles.title: ICE arrests reached record highs this summer as enforcement tactics shifted
articles.summary: In August alone, ICE officers and agents arrested a record-breaking 50,925 people, with the largest number of arrests taking place in Texas and Florida.
articles.body: The Trump administration reached a record number of immigration-related arrests over the last three months, even as the dramatic increase did not mirror the militarized spectacle seen at the start of the year. The tactics over the summer instead focused on street arrests and working with local jails and local law enforcement, with sweeps hitting cities like Houston, New York, Memphis, San Francisco and Atlanta. Immigration officers have also focused on arrests at airports, courthouses and ICE check-ins. In August alone, ICE officers and agents arrested a record 50,925 people, according to the Department of Homeland Security. That new high came on the heels of 50,208 arrests in July, which was the record at the time, according to DHS. Officers made nearly 44,000 arrests in June. These arrests follow a recent mandate to ICE field offices to arrest 2,000 people per day nationwide. ICE in August averaged around 1,600 arrests per day; ICE officers were arresting around 1,000 people a day before the mandate. The recent increase is part of a “new normal” that ICE hopes to maintain, a source familiar with the arrest operations said earlier this summer. “The hard-working men and women of DHS continue to break records as they defend the homeland and protect the American people,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement. “For the third straight month, ICE set a new record for the highest number of illegal aliens arrested in a single month, nearly 51,000.” In the winter, DHS sent large law enforcement operations to Democratic cities, culminating in the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January in Minneapolis. Their deaths led to protesters flooding the streets in Minnesota and cities like New York, Chicago and Los Angeles. After the wave of anti-ICE criticism from residents and lawmakers, DHS underwent a regime change, with border czar Tom Homan taking over from ousted DHS Secretary Kristi Noem at the time and the removal of Gregory Bovino from the position of Border Patrol commander at large. Now tactics have shifted away from flooding cities with targeted and branded operations. Yet monthly arrests reached more than 10,000 in July in Texas alone, along with more than 5,500 in Florida, more than 2,000 in Arizona and more than 1,800 in New Jersey, according to the Deportation Data Project. In Memphis, 120 people were arrested during a single raid last month. “Arrests this summer have continued to increase basically unabated,” said Juan Proaño, the CEO of the League of United Latin American Citizens. The states that saw the largest number of arrests were Texas and Florida, according to data from the Deportation Data Project, an initiative by the University of California, Berkeley, and the University of California, Los Angeles, to track ICE arrests and detentions. Both Texas and Florida have seen increasing cooperation with local law enforcement. There were 10,331 ICE arrests in Texas in July, compared with 5,787 in July of last year, and 5,501 arrests in Florida in July, compared with 1,938 last year. The surges also occurred in California, New York and New Jersey, all Democratic states. The Deportation Data Project found that there were not only a record number of arrests in communities in recent months, but also a jump in ICE requests for local jails to hold people on its behalf. Arrests also increased in areas where local police can perform some immigration enforcement duties. An increasing majority of those arrested did not have criminal convictions, according to the Deportation Data Project. In July, 73.5% of people arrested by ICE did not have criminal convictions compared with 62.6% last year, according to the Deportation Data Project. Meanwhile, 24.8% had convictions for nonviolent crimes and 1.6% had convictions for violent crimes this year, versus 34.5% and 2.9% last year.

articles.title: New York Times accused of framing Muslims as true victims of 9/11 in anniversary coverage
articles.summary: The New York Times faced accusations of framing Muslim Americans as the true victims of 9/11, but the paper calls the criticism "disingenuous."
articles.body: The New York Times on Friday was accused of treating Muslims as the true victims of the terror attacks of Sept. 11, 2021, but the paper insists any criticism is a "disingenuous" attempt to stoke outrage. "The Times can't remember 9/11 without bemoaning a ‘wave of hate’ and ‘anti-Muslim prejudice," NewsBusters executive editor Tim Graham told Fox News Digital. The Times’ published a story, "After 9/11, Islamophobia Shaped a Generation of Muslim New Yorkers," that said the "attacks unleashed a wave of hate, but the years since have seen Muslim Americans’ political and cultural influence grow." LIBERAL VIRGINIA SCHOOL DISTRICT: DON'T LINK 9/11 TERROR ATTACKS TO 'ISLAM OR MUSLIMS' Times reporters Liam Stack and Maya King wrote about "once-friendly neighbors" allegedly keeping their distance from American Muslims on the heels of the terror attacks, suggesting that many "have faced a quarter-century of suspicion and hostility." "In New York, a generation of Muslim New Yorkers responded to the Islamophobia by organizing their communities: Mosques hosted makeshift legal clinics. Small businesses became hubs in a citywide civil rights network. Muslims of different racial, ethnic and linguistic backgrounds formed alliances the city had not seen before," Stack and King wrote. "Their political organizing helped, years later, to elect the city’s first Muslim mayor, Zohran Mamdani," they continued. "But anti-Muslim prejudice still endures, echoing the Islamophobia that arose in the earliest days after Sept. 11." The Times’ story, published hours before the somber anniversary of the attacks that killed 2,977 people at the World Trade Center in New York City, the Pentagon and aboard United Flight 93 near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, said the attacks also "left many Muslim American communities scarred by heavy-handed law enforcement tactics and the suspicion, if not outright hostility, of classmates, co-workers, elected officials and cable news commentators who blamed all Muslims for the terrorism they, too, had experienced that day." MAMDANI FACES GROWING 9/11 BACKLASH AS OLD POST RESURFACES AHEAD OF GROUND ZERO CEREMONY: 'IS THIS REAL?' The Times then spoke with Afaf Nasher, the executive director of the New York chapter of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, who said that Muslim Americans were "pushed against the wall" and were faced with the decision to "run in fear" or push back. "Political empowerment was certainly one way that we are pushing back," Nasher told the Gray Lady. Stack and King noted that the ascendance of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani "has turned New York into perhaps the most prominent example of American Muslim success in the post-9/11 world" before suggesting Muslims in the United States continue to face many challenges. "Those include a history of police surveillance, backlash faced by high-profile Muslims in politics or the arts and attacks on Islamic religious expression, including the construction of mosques and the wearing of religious clothing like hijabs. Those biases have also affected followers of other faiths, in particular observant Sikh men, whose turbans are often mistaken for a form of Islamic dress," Stack and King wrote. MAMDANI HEADS TO 9/11 MEMORIAL DESPITE 110,000-SIGNATURE PUSH FROM VICTIMS’ FAMILIES TO STAY AWAY "After Sept. 11, many Muslims in New York found themselves under covert police surveillance," they continued. The report evoked a Pew Research Center survey that found some American adults believe Muslims are less patriotic than other Americans, and they often cite the Sept. 11 attacks as the reason. "By some measures, the survey showed that public attitudes toward Islam were more negative now than they were immediately after the attacks," Stack and King wrote. Graham, who has put a spotlight on bias in the media for decades, said that "any surveillance of Muslims or mosques is treated as prejudice despite the obvious point that some mosques and their leaders support Islamist terrorism." CBC RELEASES POLICY CHANGE AFTER CONTROVERSY ABOUT REFUSING TO REFER TO 9/11 AS ‘TERRORIST ATTACKS’ "’Islamophobia’ is always an oppressive problem that America needs to overcome, and increasing political and cultural influence of Muslim leftists like Zohran Mamdani was treated like signs of progress. For people who claim to oppose organized hate, they can't seem to find any in Muslim circles," Graham said. Overall, you're only presented with pro-Muslim gush," Graham continued. "There is no opposing point of view, just a citation of hatred and prejudice from Trump and the Republicans." Graham and other critics pointed out that the Times published a second story on Islamophobia on Friday, with the other one headlined, "Facing Islamophobia, Mamdani Keeps Focus on 9/11 Victims." Conservative critics took to social media to blast the Times. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Times stood by its reporting. "This misleading statement is nothing more than a disingenuous attempt to seek attention and stoke outrage by misrepresenting The New York Times's journalism covering the anniversary and commemoration of the Sept. 11 attacks," a New York Times spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "In the 25 years since that day, we have led the way on reporting on the event, its human toll, and resulting societal shifts. Audiences can see for themselves The Times's coverage now, which features a deep and diverse set of journalism reflecting on a globally significant event."

articles.title: Domestic violence allegations raise questions about holdout juror in Lindsay Clancy trial
articles.summary: The NBC10 Boston Investigators are uncovering new details about the lone holdout juror from the Lindsay Clancy murder trial.
articles.body: The NBC10 Boston Investigators are uncovering new details about the lone holdout juror from the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. Court documents and interviews with family members reveal a history of domestic violence allegations. We discovered a pending eviction case tied to months of not paying rent. The NBC10 Boston Investigators also found an active restraining order against him, while he was listening to evidence in the case. Those details raise questions about the jury selection process and how the Plymouth County resident was picked for the high-profile case that ended in a mistrial. NBC10 Boston has repeatedly attempted to contact the juror at home, where his landlord is currently trying to evict him. We are not identifying him at this time because he has chosen not to speak publicly and the jury list is currently impounded. However, we wanted to share the details that experts say should have raised red flags about how he filled out his juror questionnaire. In September of 2021, the holdout juror in the Clancy case faced a criminal charge for assaulting his wife out of Brockton District Court. According to a police report, the juror’s 13-year-old nephew called 911 after he said his uncle grabbed his wife by the throat and threw her into a dresser. The report says the juror’s mom repeatedly screamed, “You’re evil!” as police arrested him. Court records show the couple divorced after the incident and the criminal charge was later dismissed. The ex-wife told NBC10 Boston this week that she did not want to testify in the case because she was worried about losing custody of her daughter. Last year, that same teenage nephew referenced in the 2021 incident took out a restraining order after he said the juror pushed him to the ground and repeatedly punched him in the face. The teen wrote in his affidavit that his uncle then said, “You ruined my (expletive) life,” for calling the police and added, “You’ve had this coming your way for a long time.” That restraining order was still active when the juror was selected for the Clancy trial and listened to evidence for weeks in the controversial case. “I don’t see how they would’ve allowed him to be a member of this jury,” NBC10 Boston’s chief legal analyst Michael Coyne said. The standard juror questionnaire in Massachusetts clearly asks if someone has been arrested, charged with a crime or been served with a court order. All of those boxes should have been checked by this juror. “I don’t see how, if those questions had been answered correctly, one side or the other would’ve taken the chance with allowing him to be seated,” Coyne said. The NBC10 Boston Investigators also learned that the holdout juror hasn’t paid the monthly rent at his home since last March, according to housing court records. As jurors deliberated last week, the landlord secured a judgment of more than $12,000 in unpaid rent and is moving forward with an eviction, housing court records show. When the Clancy trial ended with no verdict, several jurors described how the lone holdout refused to engage in deliberations, describing him as “arrogant” and saying he wouldn’t interact with them. One juror described the holdout juror’s behavior as “shocking.” When the NBC10 Boston Investigators contacted the holdout juror’s family members, they said he had been estranged since the incident with his nephew. None of them knew about his involvement with the Clancy trial. One family member described him as a “narcissist” who she believes never should have served as a juror in such an important case. In the wake of these revelations, Coyne said he thinks the holdout juror’s questionnaire will have to be reviewed by prosecutors to see if the information the juror put down was truthful. “It is, in fact, a crime not to do so,” he said. NBC10 Boston has reached out to the Plymouth District Attorney’s Office to ask about our findings, along with Clancy’s defense team. Both sides declined to comment on Friday afternoon. Juror questionnaires are not public records, so it’s unclear if the document in question still exists or if it was destroyed in the wake of the mistrial. Because of that, NBC10 Boston cannot confirm how the juror filled out the questionnaire.
